utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is Case Number IT-04-82-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ljube Boskoski and Johan Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. I would like to welcome you to this Status Conference. Can I ask the accused whether you understand the proceeding in your own language. Mr. Boskoski, do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BOSKOSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And Mr. Tarculovski?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I ask for the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dan Saxon for the Prosecution, with my colleague Mr. Anees Ahmed, and our case manager Ms. Salla Moilanen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And appearances for the Defence, for Mr. Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Pursuant to the authority of lead counsel Dragan Godzo, I am appearing here on behalf of Mr. Boskoski. My name is Edina Residovic, co-counsel, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: You are accompanied by whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jesenka Residovic, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And the counsel for Mr. Tarculovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour. For the accused Johan Tarculovski, his chief attorney, Defence counsel Antonio Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think you have been informed about special arrangements with regard to use of the microphones, so I don't have to repeat it. I hope so. Before we start, perhaps I may also, for the public, a little bit explain what the purpose of this meeting is. Pursuant to Rule 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of our Tribunal, a Trial Chamber shall convene a Status Conference within 120 days of the initial appearance of the accused, and thereafter within 120 days of the last Status Conference, in order to organise exchanges between the parties so as to ensure an expeditious preparation for trial, and to review the status of the accused's case and to allow the accused the opportunity to raise issues in relation thereto, including the mental and physical condition and matters relating to detention. The last Status Conference took place on December 12th of the last year, and as is usually the case, in preparation of this Status Conference there was held a Rule 65 ter meeting earlier this morning. It was performed by Mr. Herman von Hebel, and he has briefed me about the discussion at the conference, so I would not repeat everything that has been discussed at the 65 ter meeting but only those issues which seem to be relevant to be discussed here in this public appearance. Now, the first point which I would like to address is the indictment and the issue of the pre-trial briefs. I would like to recall that on the 5th of December, 2005, the Prosecution filed a new indictment containing amendments ordered by the Trial Chamber and amendments submitted by the Prosecution. On November 1, 2005, the Trial Chamber issued a decision granting most of the changes and amendments, while rejecting two newly proposed amendments. And in course of these amendments, on November 2, 2005, an amended indictment was filed in compliance with the Trial Chamber's decision. And on November 7th of the last year, the Prosecution filed its pre-trial brief. It appeared there that there was still a contradiction between the latest version of the indictment and the pre-trial brief, as to way the command responsibility for the accused Boskoski was formulated. There was no time then to try to resolve that issue, so the issue had been taken up again in a 65 ter meeting on the 23rd of March, 2006, regarding further discrepancies in the amended indictment and the pre-trial brief. Now, as a result of this meeting of April -- of this meeting on April 4 - that means a couple of days ago - a motion for leave to amend the indictment has been brought in by the Prosecution. In the meantime, we received a motion by the counsel of Mr. Tarculovski and also just the other day for the counsel by Mr. Boskoski. Now, what I would like to ask the Prosecution, whether you want to bring in a reply to these responses by the Defence counsels.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution only received the response of the accused Boskoski shortly after 9.00 this morning. With leave of the Trial Chamber, in order to provide a coherent and hopefully concise reply, we would ask your leave to file a reply in the next day or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yes, okay. This -- you will have time to reply at the end of the week. That would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: -- on Friday. And then there will have to be taken a decision by the Trial Chamber -- provided by the Trial Chamber. Thank you. Any further remarks on this point? If this is not the case, we can continue with addressing some outstanding motions. The first motion which I would like to address is the Prosecution's motion for leave to amend its original Rule 65 ter witness list dated November 7, 2005, with Annexes A and B filed on the 31st of March, 2006. The Prosecution is requesting to remove seven witnesses and to add five witnesses. So far no responses have been filed by the Defence, and I would like to ask the Defence whether you are still considering to file a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to say that the expert reports of these witnesses were disclosed to us not so long ago, and we have to bear in mind the deadlines that we have, so as long as that is not neglected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And you are aware that the deadline had been, I think, the 14th of April. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Which deadline?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: The deadline for your response was to be -- supposed to be filed by April 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we responded to the motion to amend the indictment. As for the list of witnesses, yes, the 14th of April could be the deadline, but if you agree, what we stated orally today can be taken as a written response. If you, however, request otherwise, then, yes, we can comply with your request and provide a written response by the 14th of April concerning the amended list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Of course we can accept this as your written response, but then I misunderstood you a little bit. I thought that you would sort of bring in a further written statement. But if it is not the case, then we consider your oral statement here as your response which has been filed within the time given to you; that means prior to April 14th.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We agree for these four out of five proposed witnesses to be put on the witness list. However, as for their expert status, we will provide our response concerning that once we respond to their expert reports in accordance with Rule 94 bis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I am clear about that. Thank you. Now, the Trial Chamber will issue its decision in the near future on this motion. The next motion which I would like to address is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, you -- the Prosecution wants to make a submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, I was just made aware of the following problem: Perhaps you should be a little bit cautious as mentioning names here, otherwise we should go into private session. So if you find a way not to mention names, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With regard to the witness referred to by my learned colleague a few minutes ago, I would simply make the following observations: It is true that the Prosecution omitted to place this witness on its original witness list filed on 7th of November. Prosecution has been completely honest about that fact. However, having said that, Your Honour, as we know, there is still no date set yet for the commencement of this trial. The statement of this witness has been disclosed to the Defence, both in English and in the language of the accused. And certainly there would be no prejudice suffered by either of the Prosecution [sic] if a -- if this witness was added to the list at that time. On the contrary, since a trial is a search for the truth, in the Prosecution's submission, the addition of this witness would assist the Chamber and the parties in finding the full truth about the charges alleged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At this moment I just would like to say that we will take into consideration both the response of the Defence and the reply by the Prosecution when we have to take our decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So what I just did was to redact the transcript to remove the names of the witnesses which have been put here, to be on the safe side, so to say. Now, the next issue would be the confidential Prosecution's third motion for admission of written statements in lieu of viva voce testimony pursuant to Rule 92 bis and the attached annexes. The Prosecution has requested to admit the written statement of two witnesses pursuant to Rule 92 bis of the Rules. This is a third and last motion of three relating to admissions of written statements pursuant to this rule. The motion consists of only two statements. One statement relates to a witness who was only recently suggested to be admitted -- added to the witness list. The Defence have not been provided before with a copy of the statement. The Defence of Boskoski filed a motion on the 7th of April to have until 17th of April - 14 days - to respond. And the Defence counsel of Mr. Tarculovski requested extra time until the 24th April to respond. Now, as it was already discussed, I think, in the 65 ter meeting, the Pre-Trial Chamber will first take a decision on the Prosecution's motion for leave to amend its original Rule 65 ter witness list which had been filed on the 31st of March. And then the Pre-Trial Chamber intends to do so in the course of this week. And from the day of issuing this decision, the parties will be provided 14 days to file a response to the third Rule 92 bis motion. That's what I would like you to inform about. Is there any comment from your side? If it is not the case, the next issue would be the Defence Boskoski -- the motion on behalf of the -- of Mr. Boskoski for access to confidential material in the Haradinaj case dated 6th of April, 2006. As you have already been informed in the 65 ter meeting, the Trial Chamber will take the decision in due course. Now, the next -- any comment of this? If not the case, I turn to the Defence motion pursuant to Rule 94 bis of expert reports which has been filed on the 6th of April this year. Now, as you may recall from the 65 ter meeting, there has been some discussion on the translation of these expert reports. And may I ask the Defence why it appears so important, first, to have translated all this material.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have requested the Trial Chamber to consider our application, bearing in mind the rights of the accused as defined in Article 21 of the Statute. The accused has the right to receive evidence in the language that he speaks and understands, evidence against him in his case. We consider the expert reports to be very significant evidence in the hands of the Prosecution. The Prosecution is using those reports to prove the culpability of our client. That is why our reading of Article 21 of the Statute is such that before any deadlines for responses to those expert reports can start, the accused have to be able to read the reports. I have to say that there is a certain jurisprudence in this Tribunal in that regard, and I have also mentioned my experience from the Hadzihasanovic case at our 65 ter meeting. The Trial Chamber there also allowed the Defence, based on Article 21 of the Statute, and decided that the deadline would start from the date that the expert report is translated into the language of the accused. I think that it's a rather elementary request that an accused should know the evidence in his own language, evidence against him; and my other argument is that there is already jurisprudence of this Tribunal in that regard. That is why I think that you should accept these arguments and adjust our deadline for submitting the response to the expert report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any response from the OTP side?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution yesterday filed a written response, and we have nothing to add to that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. I have been informed that the translation of these reports which are in issue is expected early May, so I think the time for response will be by mid-June, something like this, and we will take it into our overall scheduling order, which is due to be issued hopefully so at the end -- before the end of this week. Now, the next point which I would like to raise is the disclosure -- are disclosure matters. Since most of it has been dealt with in the 65 ter meeting, I would only like to address the exhibits problem. I -- as far as I have been informed, out of the fifty -- 556 exhibits, there are still about 30 exhibits not translated yet, not including the exhibits relating to the expert reports. Again, I have been informed that the translation of these exhibits is expected until the end of April. Is this still the case or is there any change with this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is still the case, Your Honour. I must say, the Prosecution is dependent on the fine efforts of CLSS in this regard, but we have asked to have these materials no later than the end of this month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. So it's only just to mention this and to make it clear that we are at least trying to have this also finalised as soon as possible. Now, the next issue would be the problem of agreed facts. You may recollect that, according to the scheduling order of 15th of December last year, the parties were required to finalise discussions on first and second agreed facts proposals by May 5th, 2006. A first set of agreed facts was sent to the Defence on the 19th of August, 2005, and the second one on the 2nd of November, 2005. By letter of April 10, the Prosecution informed the Chamber that it had only received a response from counsel for Mr. Boskoski in October 2005, and the parties have also regularly indicated that they are in a good position to enter into discussion on agreed facts once disclosure is finalised. Now, as I will do with other issues, this matter will also be dealt with with regard to a new deadline within the overall scheduling order to be issued in due course. The next -- is there any comment from any side? No. So I will -- now I would like to come to the length of the proposed trial. This, of course, is a very important problem and concern, particularly with regard to the completion strategy of our Tribunal. By reviewing the current proposed witness list of the Prosecution, we have about 123 witnesses. If we calculate the time which is indicated for the examination-in-chief of these witnesses, we come to a total viva voce evidence of approximately 230 hours, not including cross-examination. Since a normal sitting day is for three hours and 45 minutes, this equals a total, approximately, of 61 sitting days for only the presentation of the Prosecution witnesses without the cross-examination. And now if I calculate that the cross-examination by the two accused, by the Defence, may take approximately the same amount of time, this would run up that the Prosecution case will last at least 120 sitting days, and that makes approximately 24 weeks or roughly six months. And this calculation there's still not included Rule 92 bis witnesses, which also may need some sort of cross-examination, at least perhaps some of them. Now, taking everything together we come to a total of 164 days for the Prosecution case, which would mean between seven to eight months. Now, taking into account that the indictment relates to a time period of only a few days, seven to eight months means quite a lot if not too much. And if we also recollect that the Prosecution had foresaw or indicated that the Prosecution case would roughly take up about four months in total, now we would have a doubling of the original four months. Now, may I ask the Prosecution whether we have some -- can give some explanation for this quite tremendous expansion in time, and perhaps I may connect my question with asking you whether you see possibilities to cut down, at least to a certain degree, what is now the calculation; or do you think that our calculation is not realistic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution does not question the calculations of the Chamber, Your Honour. The Prosecution has more recently had more time to reflect upon the length of its case, and that is why we have provided the numbers that we have provided in its more recent submissions. In response to your question as to whether it would be possible to cut down the length of the Prosecution's case, I believe there is some room, Your Honour, and the Prosecution will abide by any order relevant to that issue issued by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Of course the final -- as you all are aware, the final decision has to be taken in the pre-trial conference, but it is also possible to direct it before the pre-trial conference. And I would be -- appreciate it very much if you would -- for the next Status Conference that you might indicate what possibilities you see to cut -- cut it down, or what other -- indicate whether the time with which you have foreseen for the examination-in-chief may be cut down to a certain degree. So if -- I think there are two possibilities: Either cutting down the witness list or perhaps trying to cut down the time which will be needed for the examination-in-chief, and then come up with a new calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution will certainly do that by the time we meet again for our next Status Conference, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. These are the points I wanted to raise. Are there any other issues you would like to address at this moment? From the Defence I see nothing. From the OTP, no -- then I would like to ask, and it is my duty, my official duty, to ask the accused whether they would wish to raise any matter relating to their state of health or the condition of detention. Now, Mr. Boskoski, would you like to address this point? Is there anything you would like to mention with regard to the state of your health or your condition of detention at this point now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BOSKOSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with respect to the detention condition, everything is fine. The attitude of the personnel, of the medical personnel, we have to mention that we are pleased and I do not have any objections with respect to the accommodation, detention. However, I have had some health problems due to the overall situation that we have faced over the past period and -- but with a very good medical intervention, my medical condition at this moment is good and I'm feeling good. I do not have anything else to add, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Boskoski. Mr. Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Please switch on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have anything to complain. The situation in the prison and detention is good. My health condition is well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, we would like to inform you that you may raise matters relating to your condition to the commanding officer of the Detention Unit and the Registrar pursuant to the Rules governing the detention of persons awaiting trial or appeal. I also would like to assure you, as far as it is in my disposal, I would also be prepared to take up matters if you would like to address me too. So if there is no other issue at this moment, the court now will be adjourned. Thank you very much, and may you have a good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: adjourned at 12.08 p.m.
